title: SynLat: Syntax-Aligned Text–Latent Compression for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

paper.title: SynLat: Syntax-Aligned Text–Latent Compression for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces impose substantial output-token costs. Under
constrained budgets, compression must preserve answer-critical information,
making boundary placement central. Token-level and fixed-length boundaries can
fragment coherent spans such as phrases, formulas, and local derivations,
whereas step-level boundaries can bind content requiring different compression
actions. We introduce SynLat, a text–latent CoT framework that aligns
compression boundaries with syntactic structure through non-overlapping
Syntax-Aligned Units (SAUs). An answer-conditioned Teacher constructs
progressive KEEP/LATENT targets for a single compression-conditioned Student,
which generates mixed reasoning from only the question and requested
compression level at inference. Across two Qwen3 Student scales, Standard- and
Long-CoT groups, and three compression levels, SynLat matches or exceeds the
strongest evaluated baseline in all 12 task-group aggregates and strictly leads in 11
under the reported achieved-CR selection protocol. Overall gains reach 3.6/2.6
points at MEDIUM and 7.0/5.5 points at HIGH for Qwen3-8B/14B, with larger
advantages under stronger compression, particularly on Long-CoT groups.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting makes intermediate reasoning explicit [ 17 ] , but long traces increase output-token cost. Explicit compression methods include token pruning [ 19 ] , chunk compression [ 16 ] , step-entropy filtering [ 9 ] , and formula preservation [ 14 ] . At aggressive ratios, however, deleting or condensing text can reduce logical fidelity and fragment symbolic expressions [ 14 ] . Figure 1: Compression-decision boundaries for the same reasoning sentence. Token and fixed-window units can fragment local relations, whereas step-level units can bind distinct relations; Syntax-Aligned Units preserve coherent relations while keeping them separately assignable to text or latent form. Latent compression instead moves reasoning into non-text carriers. COCONUT propagates hidden states as continuous reasoning states [ 4 ] , whereas CODI distills explicit CoT into continuous space [ 11 ] . With the trace fully replaced, latent states must carry complete, precise derivations without textual anchors. Moreover, SIM-CoT reports that scaling implicit reasoning can destabilize training as latent representations become homogeneous and lose semantic diversity [ 18 ] . Hybrid methods therefore retain selected text: Token Assorted mixes it with discrete latent symbols [ 12 ] , while SPOT replaces selected spans with pause states [ 2 ] . Compression then becomes a representation-fidelity allocation problem: which content remains textual and which becomes latent. However, this allocation requires suitable decision units, and existing methods expose a boundary mismatch. As Figure 1 illustrates, token and fixed-window units can fragment local relations, whereas step-level units can bind distinct relations into one compression decision. Neither provides trace-specific units that keep local relations intact while leaving them separately assignable to text or latent form. Constituency syntax supplies nested contiguous spans for such allocation units [ 8 ] . SynLat converts them into ordered, non-overlapping Syntax-Aligned Units (SAUs). Offline, an answer-conditioned Teacher assigns progressive KEEP / LATENT targets, and latent units map to a shared discrete codebook. Plan-then-Generate training transfers this supervision to a compression-conditioned Student. At inference, the Student receives only the question and requested compression level, generating a mixed CoT of retained text and latent symbols before the final answer. Experiments show that, under the reported achieved compression rate (CR) selection protocol, SynLat improves the accuracy–compression trade-off, with larger gains under stronger compression, particularly on Long-CoT groups. Controlled studies further support SAU boundaries, answer-conditioned planning, and Student-side transfer. Our contributions are threefold: (i) we formulate budgeted CoT compression as a representation-fidelity allocation problem, retaining answer-critical reasoning as text while compressing recoverable content into latent representations; (ii) we introduce SynLat, which aligns text–latent allocation boundaries with trace-specific syntax and transfers answer-conditioned targets to a single Student; and (iii) experiments establish its accuracy–compression gains across the evaluated model scales, task groups, and compression levels under the reported achieved-CR selection protocol. Figure 2: Overview of SynLat. Offline target construction converts a reference trace into mixed-CoT targets through SAU construction, KEEP/LATENT allocation, and latent-code assignment; at deployment, the Student uses only the question and compression condition.

sections.heading: 2 RELATION TO PRIOR WORK
sections.text: Explicit CoT and visible compression. Chain-of-thought prompting exposes intermediate reasoning [ 17 ] , whose growing traces motivate compression within natural language. TokenSkip prunes tokens [ 19 ] ; R1-Compress condenses chunks [ 16 ] ; step-entropy filtering selects steps by entropy [ 9 ] ; and Extra-CoT preserves formulas at aggressive ratios [ 14 ] . These methods remain within visible text and delete or rewrite predefined units, motivating representations beyond text. Latent and hybrid text–latent reasoning. Latent methods move reasoning beyond ordinary text. COCONUT propagates continuous hidden states [ 4 ] , while CODI distills explicit CoT into continuous space [ 11 ] . SIM-CoT reports that scaling implicit reasoning can destabilize training and homogenize latent states [ 18 ] . DLR learns a discrete vocabulary from rendered CoT features [ 1 ] . Hybrid methods therefore retain textual anchors: Token Assorted mixes text with discrete symbols [ 12 ] , SPOT replaces spans with pause states [ 2 ] , Selective Latent Thinking gates latent spans by confidence [ 20 ] , and A*-Thought-V2 geometrically selects step-level continuous states [ 23 ] . Prior summarization work uses constituency parses to define deletable spans [ 22 ] . SynLat differs by flattening trace-specific syntax into ordered, non-overlapping SAUs and learning compression-conditioned text–latent allocation over a shared discrete codebook.

sections.heading: 3.2 Syntactic constituency structure
sections.text: Figure 3: Syntactic constituency parsing and SAU construction. A reasoning sentence is parsed into nested contiguous spans, then partitioned into non-overlapping Syntax-Aligned Units for text–latent allocation. Constituency parsing represents sentences as nested contiguous spans [ 8 ] . Applied sentence-wise, a parser maps R R to trees T s = ( V s , E s ) T_{s}=(V_{s},E_{s}) with token leaves and internal nodes v ∈ V s v\in V_{s} covering spans C v = w a ⁡ ( v ) : b ⁡ ( v ) C_{v}=w_{a(v):b(v)} . SynLat uses these boundaries rather than syntactic labels to define allocation units finer than full reasoning steps. As Figure 3 illustrates, the hierarchical, overlapping spans are flattened into ordered, non-overlapping Syntax-Aligned Units (SAUs).

sections.heading: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.text: Models, data, and benchmarks. We evaluate Qwen3-8B/14B Students [ 24 ] on MATH-500 [ 6 , 10 ] , StrategyQA [ 3 ] , OlympiadBench [ 5 ] , WorldTree V2 [ 21 ] , and ProofWriter [ 13 ] . Pre-answer lengths of correct, uncompressed development CoTs define Standard-CoT (MATH-500 and StrategyQA) and Long-CoT (the other tasks). A frozen Qwen3-235B checkpoint supplies correct-answer traces; a frozen Qwen3-235B Teacher constructs offline KEEP/LATENT targets. Supervision uses official training splits when available and otherwise disjoint external/synthetic corpora; evaluation instances and their reference solutions are excluded from target construction, codebook fitting, and model selection. Table 1 reports answer accuracy and achieved CR for both Student scales. Baselines and evaluation protocol. References are No CoT (100% CR), Raw Full CoT (uncompressed), and Ours-NONE (same-Student, 0% CR). Compression baselines are TokenSkip, Token Assorted, and SPOT [ 19 , 12 , 2 ] , which respectively prune text, mix text with latent tokens, and replace spans with latent states. They share Student scales, trace pool, splits, validation-only selection, and decoding. Ablations are dedicated Qwen3-8B studies macro-averaged over all five benchmarks. sections.heading: 5 RESULTS
sections.text: Main results. Under the reported achieved-CR selection protocol, Table 1 shows aggregate accuracy gains for SynLat at MEDIUM and HIGH across both Student scales, increasing with compression. At MEDIUM, it exceeds the strongest evaluated baseline overall by 3.6 and 2.6 percentage points for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, respectively. At HIGH, the margins widen to 7.0 and 5.5 points. For Qwen3-8B at HIGH, the margin is 4.7 points on Standard-CoT and 8.5 points on Long-CoT. Baselines outperform SynLat on MATH-500 for Qwen3-8B at LOW, ProofWriter for Qwen3-14B at LOW, and StrategyQA for Qwen3-14B at MEDIUM. Compression-unit ablation. At approximately 44% achieved CR, Table 2 shows that SAUs retain 94.0% of NONE accuracy. Fixed 5-token windows trail by 2.6 points, showing that a similar length cap is insufficient; guarded windows still trail by 1.8 points, so simple boundary protection does not recover syntax-aligned allocation. Steps trail by 4.4 points despite low split rates, indicating that coarse units hinder selective compression. SAUs therefore best balance formula preservation and granularity among the tested unit definitions for mixed text–latent compression. Token Deletion is not a pure boundary control because it also changes the compressed representation. Planning and training ablations. On fixed SAUs, answer-conditioned planning retains 94.0%/89.3% of NONE accuracy at MEDIUM/HIGH, versus 92.0%/86.2% for the strongest answer-free alternatives. Removing action-plan supervision reduces mean accuracy across the three compressed levels from 73.1 to 70.6, supporting the planning-and-transfer design.

sections.heading: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.text: In this paper, we revisit CoT compression as a problem of allocating limited representation fidelity. We propose SynLat, a text–latent compression framework that bases compression decisions on Syntax-Aligned Units, allowing local reasoning content to remain in text or be converted into latent representations according to its role. Experiments show that, under matched output budgets, SynLat achieves higher final-answer accuracy than representative compression methods, with particularly large gains on tasks that require longer reasoning traces. These results indicate that CoT compression is not only about reducing visible tokens, but also about maintaining a better match between reasoning structure and answer-relevant information during compression.

sections.heading: 7 COMPLIANCE WITH ETHICAL STANDARDS
sections.text: This study uses publicly available benchmark datasets and does not involve human or animal subjects. No ethical approval was required.

These methods remain within visible text and delete or rewrite predefined units, motivating representations beyond text. Latent and hybrid text–latent reasoning. Latent methods move reasoning beyond ordinary text. COCONUT propagates continuous hidden states [ 4 ] , while CODI distills explicit CoT into continuous space [ 11 ] . SIM-CoT reports that scaling implicit reasoning can destabilize training and homogenize latent states [ 18 ] . DLR learns a discrete vocabulary from rendered CoT features [ 1 ] . Hybrid methods therefore retain textual anchors: Token Assorted mixes text with discrete symbols [ 12 ] , SPOT replaces spans with pause states [ 2 ] , Selective Latent Thinking gates latent spans by confidence [ 20 ] , and A*-Thought-V2 geometrically selects step-level continuous states [ 23 ] . Prior summarization work uses constituency parses to define deletable spans [ 22 ] . SynLat differs by flattening trace-specific syntax into ordered, non-overlapping SAUs and learning compression-conditioned text–latent allocation over a shared discrete codebook. 3 METHOD 3.1 Preliminaries Given a question q q , standard chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning generates a textual trace R = ( w 1 , … , w n ) R=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}) before an answer y y , i.e., q → R → y q\rightarrow R\rightarrow y , where each w i w_{i} is a text token. In our discrete setting, a consecutive segment w a j : b j w_{a_{j}:b_{j}} maps to a latent token z j = ϕ ( w a j : b j ) z_{j}=\phi(w_{a_{j}:b_{j}}) , shortening the trace while discarding its natural-language form. We study mixed latent CoT, written as R ~ = ( u 1 , … , u k ) \tilde{R}=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k}) , where each u i u_{i} is a retained text span or latent token, e.g., R ~ = ( w 1 : a , z 1 , w b : d , z 2 , … ) . \tilde{R}=(w_{1:a},z_{1},w_{b:d},z_{2},\ldots). construction. A reasoning sentence is parsed into nested contiguous spans, then partitioned into non-overlapping Syntax-Aligned Units for text–latent allocation. Constituency parsing represents sentences as nested contiguous spans [ 8 ] . Applied sentence-wise, a parser maps R R to trees T s = ( V s , E s ) T_{s}=(V_{s},E_{s}) with token leaves and internal nodes v ∈ V s v\in V_{s} covering spans C v = w a ⁡ ( v ) : b ⁡ ( v ) C_{v}=w_{a(v):b(v)} . SynLat uses these boundaries rather than syntactic labels to define allocation units finer than full reasoning steps. As Figure 3 illustrates, the hierarchical, overlapping spans are flattened into ordered, non-overlapping Syntax-Aligned Units (SAUs). 3.3 SynLat: syntax-aligned text–latent CoT compression Overview. As Figure 2 illustrates, SynLat constructs mixed-CoT targets offline from a reference trace R R and answer y ∗ y^{*} through SAU construction, KEEP/LATENT allocation, and code assignment. Compression condition c c controls how many units are replaced; the Teacher selects which ones, and two-stage training transfers these targets to a Student. Tree-guided syntax-aligned unit construction. Starting at each parse root, SynLat retains nodes of at most L max L_{\max} tokens and otherwise descends to their children. Adjacent siblings sharing a parent are merged within the same cap; residual content falls back to leaf spans. Sorting retained spans by their character intervals yields S 1 : N = ( S 1 , … , S N ) S_{1:N}=(S_{1},\ldots,S_{N}) , an ordered, non-overlapping partition that fully reconstructs R R . Compression-conditioned progressive allocation. For each S i S_{i} , SynLat assigns a i ( c ) ∈ { KEEP , LATENT } a_{i}^{(c)}\in\{\mathrm{KEEP},\mathrm{LATENT}\} : KEEP preserves its text, whereas LATENT replaces it with a discrete token. Condition c c specifies a target SAU replacement ratio r ⁡ ( c ) r(c) , giving K c = ⌊ r ⁡ ( c ) ​ N ⌋ K_{c}=\lfloor r(c)N\rfloor replacements and A c = { i ∣ a i ( c ) = LATENT } A_{c}=\{i\mid a_{i}^{(c)}=\mathrm{LATENT}\} with | A c | = K c |A_{c}|=K_{c} . Unlike achieved token-level CR, this target counts units. Using y ∗ y^{*} , the offline Teacher retains answer-critical text and replaces units it judges recoverable from the remaining textual anchors and context, rather than judging local importance alone. The conditions share a progressive replaceability order, so A LOW ⊆ A MEDIUM ⊆ A HIGH A_{\mathrm{LOW}}\subseteq A_{\mathrm{MEDIUM}}\subseteq A_{\mathrm{HIGH}} : higher compression adds LATENT units without restoring earlier ones to text. Codebook construction and mixed CoT realization. LATENT units use a shared finite codebook [ 15 ] , not span-specific placeholders. SAUs from a task-independent corpus are encoded by frozen SpanBERT [ 7 ] , followed by IncrementalPCA, normalization, and spherical mini-batch k k -means to form E = { e k } k = 1 K code E=\{e_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K_{\mathrm{code}}} . We evaluate Qwen3-8B/14B Students [ 24 ] on MATH-500 [ 6 , 10 ] , StrategyQA [ 3 ] , OlympiadBench [ 5 ] , WorldTree V2 [ 21 ] , and ProofWriter [ 13 ] . Pre-answer lengths of correct, uncompressed development CoTs define Standard-CoT (MATH-500 and StrategyQA) and Long-CoT (the other tasks). A frozen Qwen3-235B checkpoint supplies correct-answer traces; a frozen Qwen3-235B Teacher constructs offline KEEP/LATENT targets. Supervision uses official training splits when available and otherwise disjoint external/synthetic corpora; evaluation instances and their reference solutions are excluded from target construction, codebook fitting, and model selection. Under the reported achieved-CR selection protocol, Table 1 shows aggregate accuracy gains for SynLat at MEDIUM and HIGH across both Student scales, increasing with compression. At MEDIUM, it exceeds the strongest evaluated baseline overall by 3.6 and 2.6 percentage points for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, respectively. At HIGH, the margins widen to 7.0 and 5.5 points. For Qwen3-8B at HIGH, the margin is 4.7 points on Standard-CoT and 8.5 points on Long-CoT. Baselines outperform SynLat on MATH-500 for Qwen3-8B at LOW, ProofWriter for Qwen3-14B at LOW, and StrategyQA for Qwen3-14B at MEDIUM. Compression-unit ablation. At approximately 44% achieved CR, Table 2 shows that SAUs retain 94.0% of NONE accuracy. Fixed 5-token windows trail by 2.6 points, showing that a similar length cap is insufficient; guarded windows still trail by 1.8 points, so simple boundary protection does not recover syntax-aligned allocation. Steps trail by 4.4 points despite low split rates, indicating that coarse units hinder selective compression. SAUs therefore best balance formula preservation and granularity among the tested unit definitions for mixed text–latent compression. Token Deletion is not a pure boundary control because it also changes the compressed representation. Planning and training ablations. On fixed SAUs, answer-conditioned planning retains 94.0%/89.3% of NONE accuracy at MEDIUM/HIGH, versus 92.0%/86.2% for the strongest answer-free alternatives. Removing action-plan supervision reduces mean accuracy across the three compressed levels from 73.1 to 70.6, supporting the planning-and-transfer design. 6 CONCLUSION In this paper, we revisit CoT compression as a problem of allocating limited representation fidelity. We propose SynLat, a text–latent compression framework that bases compression decisions on Syntax-Aligned Units, allowing local reasoning content to remain in text or be converted into latent representations according to its role. Experiments show that, under matched output budgets, SynLat achieves higher final-answer accuracy than representative compression methods, with particularly large gains on tasks that require longer reasoning traces. These results indicate that CoT compression is not only about reducing visible tokens, but also about maintaining a better match between reasoning structure and answer-relevant information during compression. 7 COMPLIANCE WITH ETHICAL STANDARDS This study uses publicly available benchmark datasets and does not involve human or animal subjects.
